opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and I think about it a bit differently from how it's usually framed.

The usual framing is that we have scaling laws: more compute, more data, bigger models, better performance. In that picture compute is the bottleneck, and the question becomes how many GPUs or TPUs you can get and how efficiently you can use them. That's certainly true to a degree. Pretraining at the frontier is extraordinarily expensive, and access to compute shapes who can do what kind of research.

But I think the more interesting constraint over the next decade isn't raw compute. It's what we spend the compute on. For a long time the recipe was to take a large, fixed dataset, mostly human-generated text from the internet, and compress it into a model. That dataset is finite. We're getting to the point where the marginal value of throwing more compute at the same static data is diminishing. So the question becomes how you turn compute into new, useful data.

That's where my interest in open-endedness comes in. If you want systems that keep improving, you need processes that generate their own learning opportunities: environments, tasks, curricula, problems that are just at the edge of what the system can currently do. Self-play is the classic example. AlphaGo didn't get superhuman by reading more human games. It got there by playing against itself and constantly generating new, harder challenges. The open question is how you do that in much broader, messier domains than board games, things like science, coding, and reasoning in the open world.

In that view, compute isn't just a resource you pour into a training run. It's the fuel for an open-ended search process. More compute lets you explore more, generate more candidate tasks and solutions, evaluate more ideas, and keep the interesting ones. So I'd argue the next decade's scaling story is more about scaling exploration and experience than scaling a single pretraining run. You can already see this with inference-time compute and reinforcement learning on top of foundation models, where letting a model think longer, try things, and learn from feedback buys you a lot.

There are real constraints, of course. Energy and hardware supply matter, and inefficient search can burn huge amounts of compute on uninteresting things. That's actually the hard research problem: how do you measure "interestingness," or novelty plus learnability, so the system spends its compute wisely? Humans are pretty good at that intuitively. Getting machines to do it well is, I think, one of the most important open problems in the field.

So my short answer: compute will remain a constraint, but the bigger lever is how intelligently we convert compute into new knowledge, rather than just how much of it we have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute as a constraint and argues for using it differently, but does not caution that the compute technology used in ten years may differ from today's.

r002.rationale: It says compute will remain a constraint, but does not predict that it will become a bottleneck within the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, compute is obviously the thing everyone points to, and I think it's genuinely important, but I'd push back a little on the framing of it as the binding constraint.

If you look at the history of the field, the big jumps haven't just come from more FLOPs. They've come from better ideas about what to do with the FLOPs. Transformers were a more compute-efficient way of using the hardware we already had. Self-play in AlphaGo, RLHF, chain-of-thought at inference time: these were algorithmic moves that changed what a given amount of compute could buy you. So my first instinct is that compute matters enormously, but the exchange rate between compute and capability is not fixed, and that exchange rate is where a lot of the interesting research lives.

The second thing I'd say is that I think we're at a point where the bottleneck is shifting from training compute to, roughly, data and environments. We've more or less exhausted the easy supply of high-quality human-written text. So the question becomes: where do the next orders of magnitude of signal come from? And my answer, which is the thing I've been working on for years, is that they come from open-endedness. Systems that generate their own curriculum, their own problems, their own environments, and then learn from them. That's an inherently compute-hungry paradigm, because you're spending compute not just on gradient updates but on search, on simulation, on generating and filtering experience. So in that sense compute matters even more than before, but it's a different kind of compute spend. It's much more about inference and environment interaction than about one giant pretraining run.

Third, I think the hardware trajectory itself is less certain than people assume. Moore's Law in the classical sense has slowed. What's kept things going is specialization, bigger chips, better interconnects, and frankly just building enormous data centers. Energy becomes a real constraint there. So if you're planning for a decade, I wouldn't bet on compute per dollar continuing to improve at the rate it did over the last ten years. Which, again, pushes you back toward algorithmic efficiency and toward paradigms where the model gets smarter about where it spends its compute.

And the last point, which I find most exciting: if you have systems that are getting good enough to do research themselves, to propose and test ideas, then compute becomes the input to an automated discovery loop. At that point, the question isn't "how much compute do we have" but "how good is the search process we're running on top of it." That's where I think the real leverage is over the next decade.

So, short version: compute is necessary, I don't think it's sufficient, and I think the field has historically underestimated how much of progress is about ideas rather than scale.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the hardware trajectory is uncertain and compute-per-dollar gains may slow, but does not clearly caution that the compute technology used for AI ten years from now may differ from today’s.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses compute costs and energy constraints over the next decade, but does not predict that compute will become a bottleneck within the next few years; it instead questions whether compute is the binding constraint.

astra-6.text:
I think compute will remain a major constraint, but I wouldn’t think of it as a fixed ceiling on progress. What matters is the interplay between the hardware we have, the algorithms we run on it, and how effectively we use that compute.

Over the next decade, we can make progress by building larger systems, but also by finding methods that learn more efficiently. If you can achieve the same capability with substantially less computation, that changes what’s feasible just as surely as getting faster hardware does. And those improvements can compound.

There are also practical constraints around power, infrastructure, and access. An idea might be promising, but if testing it requires an enormous training run, that limits who can explore it and how quickly they can iterate. So I think an important question is how we enable useful research at smaller scales while still learning what happens when we scale systems up.

I’m optimistic that we’ll continue to find better ways to use compute. I’m less confident that we can predict exactly where the bottleneck will be ten years from now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hardware and compute efficiency but does not caution that AI compute technology in ten years may differ from today’s.

r002.rationale: It calls compute a major constraint over the next decade, but does not predict that it will become a bottleneck within the next few years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute is clearly a constraint, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a fixed ceiling on progress. What matters is not just how much compute we have, but how effectively we use it. Better algorithms can change what you’re able to achieve with the same hardware quite dramatically.

There’s also a question of where we spend that compute. Do we put more into training, or do we give a system more time to reason, explore, and learn when it encounters a new problem? Those choices can lead to quite different capabilities.

Over the next decade, I’d expect progress to come from that interaction between hardware, algorithms, and how we formulate the learning problem. Compute will shape what experiments we can run and who can run them, which is a real concern. But I don’t think we can extrapolate AI progress from hardware improvements alone.
